board.text: Rectangle: length 15 cm, width 11 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 15 centimetres long and 11 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 11 rows of 15, so we multiply 15 by 11.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 11 rows of squares, and 15 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
15 times 11 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 11 into 10 and 1.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 15 times 10 is 150. And 15 times 1 is 15. Now we put the two parts together. What is 150 plus 15?
Add them up: 150 plus 15 is 165.
So the area is 165 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 165 squares shared into 11 rows gives 15 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Rectangle: length 24 cm, width 11 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 24 centimetres long and 11 centimetres wide, and we want its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 11 rows of 24, so we multiply 24 by 11.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 11 rows, with 24 in every row. So the area is length times width.
24 times 11 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 11 into 10 and 1.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 24 times 10 is 240. And 24 times 1 is 24. Now we put the two parts together. What is 240 plus 24?
240 plus 24 makes 264.
There it is: the area is 264 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 264 squares shared into 11 rows gives 24 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, width 3 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 25 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide, and we want its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 25 plus 3 is 28.
Careful: 28 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two widths, so we double it. 2 times 28 is 56.
There it is: the perimeter is 56 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 25, 3, 25, 3. Together they make 56.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

board.text: Rectangle: length 15 cm, width 9 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 15 centimetres long and 9 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 15 plus 9 is 24.
Don't stop at 24. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 24 is 48.
So the perimeter is 48 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 15, 9, 15, 9. Together they make 48.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

board.text: Rectangle: length 16 cm, width 4 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 16 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 4 rows of 16, so we multiply 16 by 4.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 4 rows of squares, and 16 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
16 times 4 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 16 into 10 and 6.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 10 times 4 is 40. And 6 times 4 is 24. Now we put the two parts together. What is 40 plus 24?
40 plus 24 makes 64.
So the area is 64 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 64 squares shared into 4 rows gives 16 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Length = 8 ft, 2 more than the width. Area = ?

spec.note: The length is 2 more than the width. Area = ?

beats.say: Here's a rectangle. Its length is 8 feet, and the length is 2 more than the width. We need the area.

ask.ifNot: The length is the bigger side here: it is 2 more than the width. So the width must be 2 less than 8.

beats.say: For area we need the length and the width. We know the length. So how wide is the rectangle?
The length is 2 more, so the width is 2 less. 8 minus 2 is 6 feet.
Careful: the 2 is not the width. It only tells us how much shorter the width is.
Now, area is length times width. 8 times 6 is 48.
So the area is 48 square feet.
Quick check: is 8 really 2 more than 6? Yes. So our sides fit the question.
The plan: find the missing side first, then multiply the two sides.

board.text: Wire: rectangle 16 cm by 12 cm, then a square. Side = ?

spec.note: The same wire is bent into a square. Side = ?

beats.say: A wire is bent into a rectangle, 16 centimetres by 12 centimetres. Then the same wire is bent into a square. How long is each side of the square?

ask.ifNot: The wire is the edge of the shape, not the space inside. The distance round the edge is the perimeter.

beats.say: The wire goes all the way round the rectangle. So the length of the wire is the rectangle's what?
One length and one width make 16 plus 12, which is 28. That is halfway round.
Double it for the whole wire. 2 times 28 is 56 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: The wire is shared equally among the 4 sides of the square. Sharing equally means dividing by 4.

beats.say: Now the same 56 centimetres is bent into a square, and a square has 4 equal sides. What do we do with 56?
56 divided by 4. Half of 56 is 28, and half of 28 is 14.
So each side of the square is 14 centimetres.
Check: 4 sides of 14 make 56, the whole wire. It fits.
Same wire means same perimeter. Find the perimeter first, then share it among the new sides.

spec.note: a is the side of a square with perimeter 28 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: A square has side a, and its perimeter is 28 centimetres. A rectangle is 3 a long and 2 a wide. We want the rectangle's area.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides, and together they make 28. So we share 28 into 4 equal parts.

beats.say: First we need a. The square's 4 equal sides add up to 28. So how long is one side?
28 divided by 4 is 7. So a is 7 centimetres.
Now the rectangle. 3 a means 3 times 7, which is 21. And 2 a means 2 times 7, which is 14.
Area is length times width: 21 times 14. Let's split 14 into 10 and 4.
21 times 10 is 210. 21 times 4 is 84. Together that makes 294.

ask.ifNot: When the working is sound, trust it. 274 is close, but close is not equal. The choice None is there for exactly this.

beats.say: Now look at the choices: 149, 274, 245, or None. Our 294 is not there! What should we do?

board.text: Area = 294 cm², so the answer is None

beats.say: Here's the trap: 274 looks a lot like 294. Never grab a number just because it is close.
Let's check our sum another way. 20 times 14 is 280, and one more 14 makes 294. Still 294.
So: find a first, build the sides, then multiply. And trust your working, even when the answer is None.

spec.note: Perimeter = 132 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: The perimeter of a square is 132 centimetres. We want its area.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides. Together they make 132, so we share 132 into 4 equal parts.

beats.say: For area we need the side. The 4 equal sides add up to 132. How do we find one side?
132 divided by 4. Half of 132 is 66, and half of 66 is 33. So each side is 33 centimetres.
Area is side times side: 33 times 33. Split one 33 into 30 and 3.
33 times 30 is 990. And 33 times 3 is 99.
Add the two parts. 990 plus 99 makes 1089.

ask.ifNot: Look back at the question: the perimeter is in centimetres. So the little squares we count are square centimetres.

beats.say: Now be careful, because two of the choices say 1089! The side was in centimetres. So which unit does the area have?
So the area is 1089 square centimetres. Always read the unit as well as the number.
Check the side: 4 times 33 is 132. That is our perimeter.
For a square: divide the perimeter by 4 to get the side. Then side times side gives the area.

board.text: Square and equilateral triangle: same perimeter
Triangle side = 12 cm. Area of square = ?

spec.note: A square has the same perimeter. Area of the square = ?

beats.say: A square and an equilateral triangle have the same perimeter. Each side of the triangle is 12 centimetres. We want the area of the square.

spec.note: Perimeter = 3 × 12 cm

beats.say: Start with the shape we know. An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides. So its perimeter is 3 times 12, which is 36.

ask.ifNot: 12 centimetres is the triangle's side. The square shares the same 36 centimetres among 4 sides, so its sides are shorter.

beats.say: The square has the same perimeter, 36 centimetres. How long is each side of the square?

spec.note: Same perimeter, shared among 4 equal sides

beats.say: 36 shared among 4 equal sides is 9. So the square's side is 9 centimetres, not 12.
Now the area. Side times side: 9 times 9 is 81.
So the area of the square is 81 square centimetres.
Check: 4 sides of 9 make 36, the same as the triangle. Good.
The trap was using 12 for the square. Same perimeter does not mean same side!

board.text: Perimeter of square = perimeter of triangle
Triangle side = 16 cm. Area of square = ?

spec.note: A square has the same perimeter. Area of the square = ?

beats.say: A square and an equilateral triangle have equal perimeters. The triangle's sides are 16 centimetres each. What is the area of the square?

ask.ifNot: The only thing the two shapes share is the perimeter. So we begin with the triangle's perimeter.

beats.say: We can't use 16 for the square. That is the triangle's side. So what should we find first?
All 3 sides of the triangle are 16 centimetres. 3 times 16 is 48.
The square has that same perimeter, 48, shared among 4 equal sides. 48 divided by 4 is 12.
Now the area of the square is side times side. 12 times 12 is 144.
So the area of the square is 144 square centimetres.
Check the perimeters. Square: 4 times 12 is 48. Triangle: 48 as well. They match.
Remember the path: triangle's perimeter, then the square's side, then the square's area.

board.text: 8 circles in a rectangle: 2 rows of 4

spec.note: One circle fits in each square. Radius = 4 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Eight equal circles sit inside a rectangle, in 2 rows of 4. They touch each other and the sides. Each radius is 4 centimetres. What is the rectangle's area?

ask.ifNot: 4 centimetres is the radius: from the centre to the edge. Right across the circle is the diameter, and that is twice as much.

beats.say: The circles are packed tight, so they tell us how big the rectangle is. How wide is one whole circle?

spec.note: The diameter is twice the radius

beats.say: Here's the trap: a circle takes up its whole diameter, not its radius. 2 times 4 is 8 centimetres.

spec.note: The length holds 4 circles side by side

beats.say: Along the length, 4 circles sit side by side. So the length is 4 times 8, which is 32 centimetres.

spec.note: The breadth holds 2 circles

beats.say: Up the side there are 2 rows. So the breadth is 2 times 8, which is 16 centimetres.
Area is length times breadth: 32 times 16. Split 16 into 10 and 6.
32 times 10 is 320. 32 times 6 is 192. Add them and we get 512.
So the area of the rectangle is 512 square centimetres.
So: change the radius to a diameter, count the circles each way, then multiply.

board.text: Which pair CANNOT be the length and breadth?

spec.note: Perimeter = 76 cm

beats.say: A rectangle has a perimeter of 76 centimetres. Four pairs of sides are offered. Which pair cannot be its length and breadth?

ask.ifNot: 76 is all four sides. One length and one breadth is only halfway round, so we halve 76.

beats.say: The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths. So what must one length and one breadth add up to?
Half of 76 is 38. So a pair fits only if it adds up to 38.
Now test each pair. 22 plus 16 is 38. That one fits.
11 plus 27 is 38. That fits too.
24 plus 16 is 40. That's not 38!
Test the last one, just to be sure. 29 plus 9 is 38. It fits.
With 24 and 16, the perimeter would be 2 times 40, which is 80, not 76.
So the pair that cannot be the sides is 24 centimetres and 16 centimetres.
Notice the word cannot. Three pairs work, and we want the one that doesn't. Always read which one the question wants.

board.text: Rectangle: breadth = 12 cm, perimeter = 52 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = 52 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: A rectangle is 12 centimetres broad, and its perimeter is 52 centimetres. We want its area.
For area we need the length too. The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths, so half of it is one length plus one breadth.

ask.ifNot: 52 is the whole way round, with two breadths in it. Use the half instead: length plus breadth is 26, so the length is 26 minus 12.

beats.say: Length and breadth together make 26. The breadth is 12. So what is the length?
26 minus 12 is 14. The length is 14 centimetres.
Now the area: length times breadth, 14 times 12. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 2 is 28.
140 plus 28 makes 168. So the area is 168 square centimetres.
Check the perimeter: 14 plus 12 is 26, and double 26 is 52. It fits.
So: halve the perimeter, take away the side you know, then multiply the two sides.

board.text: A rectangle has how many right angles?

beats.say: Here is a rectangle. How many right angles does it have?
A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a book. It measures 90 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Count them in the picture: top left, top right, bottom right, bottom left.

beats.say: Look at the picture. How many corners does a rectangle have?
4 corners. Now think of a door, or a page of your notebook. Every corner is a neat square corner.
That is what makes a rectangle a rectangle: all 4 of its angles are right angles.
If even one corner leaned over, the shape would not be a rectangle any more.
So remember: a rectangle means 4 right angles, every time.

board.text: How many diagonals does a quadrilateral have?

beats.say: Here is a quadrilateral: a shape with 4 sides and 4 corners. How many diagonals does it have?

spec.note: A diagonal joins two opposite corners

beats.say: A diagonal is a straight line joining two corners that are not next to each other. Let's draw one, from A across to C.

ask.ifNot: A and B are neighbours, and so are C and D. The line joining neighbours is a side. The corners still across from each other are B and D.

beats.say: Is there another one? Which two corners are still not joined?

board.text: A to C, B to D

spec.note: Two opposite pairs: A and C, B and D

beats.say: B and D are opposite each other. Join them, and we have a second diagonal.
Any more? Every other pair of corners, like A and B, is already joined by a side. So that is all of them.
A quadrilateral has 2 diagonals.
The trap is to say 4, because there are 4 sides. Diagonals join opposite corners, and there are only 2 opposite pairs.
Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80 degrees, 90 degrees and 100 degrees. We want the fourth angle.
Here is the key fact. The four angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees.
First add the three angles we know. 80 plus 90 is 170, and 100 more makes 270.

ask.ifNot: All four angles must make 360. Three of them already make 270. The fourth is whatever is left, so we subtract.

beats.say: Three angles make 270. All four must make 360. So how do we find the fourth?
360 minus 270 is 90. The fourth angle is 90 degrees.
Check: 80, 90, 100 and 90 add up to 360. It works.
So for a missing angle in a quadrilateral: add the three you know, and take the total from 360.

board.text: 4 equal sides, no right angles. What is it called?

spec.note: All four sides are equal. No corner is a right angle

beats.say: A shape has four sides, all equal, but none of its angles is a right angle. What is it called?

ask.ifNot: A rectangle only needs its opposite sides equal. The two shapes with all four sides equal are the square and the rhombus.

beats.say: We have two clues. Clue one: all four sides are equal. Which shapes have four equal sides?
So it is either a square or a rhombus.
Clue two: none of its angles is a right angle. A square always has four right angles. So it can't be a square.
What is left is the rhombus. Think of a square that has been pushed over, like a diamond.
So: four equal sides and no right angles means a rhombus.
When a question gives two clues, use both. The first clue narrows it down, and the second one decides.

board.text: Parallelogram: one angle = 70°. Angle next to it = ?

beats.say: One angle of a parallelogram is 70 degrees. We want the angle right next to it.
In a parallelogram, two angles next to each other always add up to 180 degrees. If one is small, its neighbour is big.

ask.ifNot: The equal angle is the one opposite, across the shape. The neighbour is different: together the two must make 180.

beats.say: So how do we find the angle next to 70 degrees?
180 minus 70 is 110.
So the angle next to it is 110 degrees.
Careful: 70 degrees is the angle opposite, not the one next door. Opposite angles are equal. Neighbours make 180.
Check: 70 plus 110 makes 180. It works.

spec.note: Rhombus. Perimeter = 52 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a rhombus is 52 centimetres. How long is each side?
What is special about a rhombus? All four of its sides are the same length, just like a square.

ask.ifNot: The 52 centimetres is shared equally among 4 sides. Sharing equally means dividing, and there are 4 sides.

beats.say: So 4 equal sides add up to 52. How do we find one side?
52 divided by 4. Half of 52 is 26, and half of 26 is 13.
So each side of the rhombus is 13 centimetres.
Check by walking round: 13, 13, 13 and 13 make 52. It fits.
Remember: a side is always shorter than the whole perimeter. For 4 equal sides, divide the perimeter by 4.

board.text: Square, side 25 cm. Lace all round, ₹3 per cm. Cost = ?

spec.note: Lace all around the edge: ₹3 for every centimetre

beats.say: A square handkerchief has sides of 25 centimetres. Lace goes all around its edge, and costs 3 rupees for every centimetre. What does the lace cost?

ask.ifNot: Lace is stitched along the edge, not spread over the cloth. The distance round the edge is the perimeter.

beats.say: First, how much lace? The lace goes all around the edge. So do we need the area or the perimeter?
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 25 is 100. So we need 100 centimetres of lace.
Each centimetre costs 3 rupees. So 100 centimetres cost 100 times 3, which is 300.
The lace costs 300 rupees.
The trap is to stop at one side. 25 times 3 is 75, but that only pays for one edge of the handkerchief.
So: all around means perimeter. Find the length first, then multiply by the price.

board.text: Wire: square of side 18 cm, then a rectangle

spec.note: The same wire makes a rectangle: length = 2 × breadth

beats.say: A wire is bent into a square of side 18 centimetres. Then the same wire makes a rectangle whose length is twice its breadth. What is the rectangle's area?
The wire's length is the square's perimeter. 4 times 18 is 72 centimetres.
Now the rectangle. Its length is twice its breadth. So one length is the same as 2 breadths.

ask.ifNot: Each length counts as 2 breadths. So round the rectangle we have 2, then 1, then 2, then 1. Add those up.

beats.say: Walk round the rectangle: length, breadth, length, breadth. Counting in breadths, how many is that altogether?
2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6. So 6 breadths use up the whole 72 centimetres of wire.
72 divided by 6 is 12. The breadth is 12 centimetres, and the length is twice that: 24.
Area is length times breadth: 24 times 12. 24 times 10 is 240, and 24 times 2 is 48.
240 plus 48 makes 288. The area of the rectangle is 288 square centimetres.
Notice the trap. The square's area is 18 times 18, a different number. Same wire means same perimeter, not same area.
Check the wire: 24 plus 12 is 36, and double 36 is 72. It fits, so 288 it is.

board.text: Garden 20 m by 14 m. Path 2 m wide all round.

spec.note: Garden inside, path all around. Area of the path = ?

beats.say: A garden is 20 metres long and 14 metres wide. A path 2 metres wide runs all around it, on the outside. What is the area of the path?
The path is like a frame round the garden. Here's a neat trick: find the big rectangle with the path, then take away the garden.

ask.ifNot: The path is at both ends of the garden. So the length grows by 2 metres at one end and 2 metres at the other.

beats.say: The path is 2 metres wide at the left end and at the right end. So how long is the big rectangle?

spec.note: 2 m on each side: add 4 m to the length and to the width

beats.say: That's the trap: the path is on both sides, so each measurement grows by 2 and 2. The length is 24 metres and the width is 18 metres.
Big rectangle: 24 times 18. 24 times 10 is 240, and 24 times 8 is 192. Together that is 432.
The garden alone is 20 times 14, which is 280.
Take the garden away from the big rectangle. 432 minus 280 is 152.
So the area of the path is 152 square metres.
For a path all round: add the path's width twice to each side, find the big area, and subtract the inside.

board.text: Floor 6 m by 4 m. Square tiles of side 50 cm.

spec.note: Square tiles of side 50 cm cover the floor

beats.say: A floor is 6 metres long and 4 metres wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 50 centimetres. How many tiles are needed?

ask.ifNot: 1 metre is 100 centimetres. 50 and 50 make 100, so two tiles fit along each metre.

beats.say: Watch the units! The floor is in metres but the tile is in centimetres. How many tiles of 50 centimetres fit along 1 metre?
Two tiles for every metre. Along the 6 metre side we fit 6 times 2, which is 12 tiles.
Along the 4 metre side we fit 4 times 2, which is 8 tiles. So the floor has 8 rows of 12 tiles.
8 rows of 12. 12 times 8 is 96.
The floor needs 96 tiles.
The trap is 6 times 4, which is 24. That counts big squares of 1 metre, and each of those holds 4 tiles. 24 times 4 is 96 again.
So: put everything in the same unit, count the tiles each way, then multiply.

board.text: Square of side 12 cm, cut into 2 equal rectangles.

spec.note: One straight cut makes two equal rectangles

beats.say: A square sheet of paper has sides of 12 centimetres. One straight cut makes two equal rectangles. What is the perimeter of each rectangle?

ask.ifNot: The cut goes through the middle of a 12 centimetre side. So that side is shared into two equal halves.

beats.say: The cut goes through the middle. One side of each piece is still 12 centimetres. What is the other side?
Half of 12 is 6. So each piece is 12 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide.
Now walk round one piece: 12, 6, 12, 6. That adds up to 36.
The perimeter of each rectangle is 36 centimetres.
Here's a surprise. The square's perimeter is 4 times 12, which is 48, and half of that is 24. But the answer isn't 24!
Why not? The cut makes a new edge of 12 centimetres on each piece. 24 plus that new 12 gives 36.
When you cut a shape, new edges appear. So find the sides of the new piece and add them up.

board.text: How many ALWAYS have 4 right angles?

beats.say: Think about four shapes: square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram. How many of them always have four right angles?
The important word is always. Let's test the shapes one at a time. Square first: four right angles, every time. Yes.
Rectangle: four right angles is what makes it a rectangle. Yes, always.

ask.ifNot: Picture the diamond on a playing card. Its four sides are equal, but its corners are not square corners.

beats.say: Now the rhombus. It has four equal sides. But does it always have right angles?
A rhombus can lean over, like a diamond. So, not always.
A parallelogram can lean over too. Not always.
Count the yeses: the square and the rectangle. That makes 2.
When you see the word always, hunt for a shape that breaks the rule. One leaning rhombus is enough to say no.

board.text: Length + 5 cm, width − 5 cm. The area?

spec.note: Length 5 cm longer, width 5 cm shorter. Area?

beats.say: A rectangle is 20 centimetres long and 15 centimetres wide. The length is made 5 centimetres longer, and the width 5 centimetres shorter. What happens to the area?
Area at the start: 20 times 15, which is 300.
Now change the sides. The length grows to 20 plus 5, which is 25. The width shrinks to 15 minus 5, which is 10.
We added 5 to one side and took 5 from the other. Do you think the area stays the same? Have a guess.
Let's find out. The new area is 25 times 10, which is 250.

ask.ifNot: Compare 300 at the start with 250 now. The new number is the smaller one.

beats.say: It changed! 300 has become 250. So what happened to the area?
300 minus 250 is 50. The area decreases by 50 square centimetres.
Here's the trap. Plus 5 and minus 5 keeps the perimeter the same, but not the area. For area, work out both and compare.

board.text: Carpet ₹150 per sq m. Strip ₹40 per m. Total = ?

spec.note: Carpet ₹150 per sq m. Wall strip ₹40 per m

beats.say: A hall is 12 metres long and 9 metres wide. Carpet costs 150 rupees for each square metre. A wooden strip along the walls costs 40 rupees for each metre. What is the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Carpet covers the space inside the room, and space inside is area. The strip along the walls is the one that uses perimeter.

beats.say: Two things to buy, and each uses a different measure. The carpet covers the whole floor. Which measure is that?
Carpet uses area: 12 times 9 is 108 square metres.
Each square metre costs 150 rupees. 100 times 150 is 15,000, and 8 times 150 is 1,200. Together that is 16,200 rupees.
The strip runs along all four walls. That is the perimeter. 12 plus 9 is 21, and double is 42 metres.
Each metre of strip costs 40 rupees. 42 times 4 is 168, so 42 times 40 is 1,680 rupees.
Add the two costs. 16,200 plus 1,680 makes 17,880.
So the total cost is 17,880 rupees.
The trap is using one measure for both. Covering a floor uses area. Going along the edge uses perimeter.

board.text: Field 30 m by 20 m. Posts every 5 m, all round.

spec.note: A post every 5 m, with one at each corner

beats.say: A field is 30 metres long and 20 metres wide. Fence posts go all around it, 5 metres apart, with one at each corner. How many posts are needed?
Posts go all the way round, so first we need the distance round. 30 plus 20 is 50, and double is 100 metres.
The posts are 5 metres apart. 100 divided by 5 is 20. So there are 20 gaps between posts.

choices: Yes, so add one more post
No, it is a closed loop
ask.ifNot: The fence goes round the field and comes back to where it began. So the last gap ends at the very first post.

beats.say: Now the tricky bit. In a straight line of posts you need one extra post at the end. But is this fence a straight line?
Round a loop, the last gap ends at the first post. So no extra post is needed. Posts and gaps are equal in number.
The field needs 20 posts.
Think of a tiny square with a post at each corner. 4 gaps, 4 posts. It is the same idea here.
So: find the distance round, divide by the gap, and for a closed loop that is your number of posts.

board.text: Wire 40 cm, bent into a rectangle. Length > breadth.

beats.say: A wire 40 centimetres long is bent into a rectangle with whole number sides, and the length is greater than the breadth. Find the largest area minus the smallest area.
The wire is the perimeter, 40 centimetres. So length plus breadth is half of that: 20.
Lots of pairs add up to 20. 19 and 1. 18 and 2. 17 and 3. All the way to 11 and 9.
Which pair gives the smallest area? Try the long thin one. 19 times 1 is only 19.

ask.ifNot: 10 and 10 would be a square, but the question says the length is greater than the breadth. The closest pair we are allowed is 11 and 9.

beats.say: As the sides get closer together, the area grows. 18 times 2 is already 36. So which pair gives the largest area?
That's the trap! 10 and 10 is not allowed, because the length must be greater. So the largest is 11 times 9, which is 99.
Now the difference. 99 minus 19 is 80.
So the difference is 80 square centimetres.
Same wire, very different areas. Thin rectangles hold little, and nearly square ones hold the most.

board.text: Wire: square of side 15 cm, then a rectangle
Length = 15 + 4 cm. What happens to the area?

spec.note: Same wire, new rectangle: length 4 cm more than 15 cm

beats.say: A wire is bent into a square of side 15 centimetres. Then it is bent into a rectangle whose length is 4 centimetres more than that. What happens to the area inside?
The wire is the square's perimeter: 4 times 15 is 60 centimetres. The rectangle uses the same 60.
The rectangle's length is 15 plus 4, which is 19. Length and breadth together are half the wire, and half of 60 is 30.

ask.ifNot: The wire has not grown. If the length takes 4 more, the breadth must give up 4. Length plus breadth must still make 30.

beats.say: So what is the breadth of the rectangle?
That's the trap. The breadth can't stay at 15. It shrinks to 30 minus 19, which is 11.
Rectangle's area: 19 times 11. 19 times 10 is 190, and one more 19 makes 209.
Square's area: 15 times 15 is 225.
225 has become 209. 225 minus 209 is 16. So the area decreases by 16 square centimetres.
Same wire, same perimeter, but a smaller area. A square holds the most space for its wire.

board.text: Park 30 m by 20 m. Two paths, each 2 m wide, cross.

spec.note: Park 30 m by 20 m. Two paths cross in the middle

beats.say: A park is 30 metres long and 20 metres wide. Two paths, each 2 metres wide, cross in the middle: one along the length, one across the width. What area do the paths cover?
Take the paths one at a time. The path along the length is 30 metres long and 2 metres wide. 30 times 2 is 60.
The path across the width is 20 metres long and 2 metres wide. 20 times 2 is 40.

choices: No: the crossing is counted twice
ask.ifNot: Look at the middle of the park, where the paths cross. That little square is part of the long path, and part of the short path too.

beats.say: 60 and 40. Can we just add them to get 100?
Here's the trap. Where they cross there is a square, 2 metres by 2 metres. It is inside both paths, so we have counted it twice.
So add the two paths, then take the crossing square away once. 60 plus 40 is 100, and 100 minus 4 is 96.
The paths cover 96 square metres.
Whenever two strips cross, the crossing piece belongs to both. Count it once, not twice.

board.text: Square garden, path 1 m wide all round.
Area of path = 40 sq m. Side of garden = ?

spec.note: Path all around a square garden. Path area = 40 sq m

beats.say: A square garden has a path 1 metre wide all around it. The path's area is 40 square metres. How long is each side of the garden?

spec.note: Each corner of the path is a square, 1 m by 1 m

beats.say: Let's cut the path into easy pieces. At each of the 4 corners sits a little square, 1 metre by 1 metre. Together the corners cover 4 square metres.
Take the corners away from the path. 40 minus 4 leaves 36 square metres.

ask.ifNot: The corners are already taken out, so we share the 36 that is left. There are 4 equal strips.

beats.say: What is left is 4 long strips, one along each side of the garden, all the same. So what is the area of one strip?
36 divided by 4 is 9. Each strip is 9 square metres.
A strip is 1 metre wide. For an area of 9 it must be 9 metres long. And that is exactly the side of the garden!
So each side of the garden is 9 metres.
The trap is 40 divided by 4, which gives 10. That forgets the corner squares.
Check: the big square is 11 by 11, which is 121. The garden is 9 by 9, which is 81. And 121 minus 81 is 40.

spec.note: Length × 2 and breadth × 3. New area = ?

beats.say: A rectangle has an area of 24 square centimetres. Its length is made 2 times as long and its breadth 3 times as long. What is the new area?
We don't know the sides, only the area. So let's pick a rectangle that works. 6 by 4 has an area of 24.
Make the length 2 times as long: 6 becomes 12. Make the breadth 3 times as long: 4 becomes 12 as well.
The new area is 12 times 12, which is 144.

ask.ifNot: Doubling the length doubles the area. Then making the breadth 3 times as long makes that 3 times bigger again.

beats.say: Now look closely. The area went from 24 to 144. How many times as big is that?
Twice as long, then 3 times as wide: that is 2 times 3, which is 6 times the area. And 24 times 6 is 144.
It works for any rectangle of area 24. The new area is 144 square centimetres.
The trap is adding 2 and 3 to get 5. When both sides stretch, the stretches multiply.

board.text: Length + 3 cm: area grows by 21 sq cm
Breadth + 2 cm: area grows by 20 sq cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: 3 cm longer: the extra strip is 21 sq cm

beats.say: Take a rectangle. Make its length 3 centimetres longer and the area grows by 21. Or make its breadth 2 centimetres longer and the area grows by 20. What is its perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The strip is stuck on the end of the rectangle, so it is as tall as the rectangle. That is the breadth.

beats.say: Think about the first change. A longer length adds a thin strip on the end. The strip is 3 centimetres one way. What is it the other way?

spec.note: Strip of 21 sq cm, 3 cm wide: breadth = 21 ÷ 3

beats.say: The strip is 3 by the breadth, and its area is 21. So the breadth is 21 divided by 3, which is 7.

spec.note: Strip of 20 sq cm, 2 cm wide: length = 20 ÷ 2

beats.say: Now the second change. A longer breadth adds a strip that is 2 centimetres by the length. Its area is 20.
So the length is 20 divided by 2, which is 10.
The rectangle is 10 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. 10 plus 7 is 17, and that is halfway round.
Double it for the whole perimeter. 2 times 17 is 34 centimetres.
Check the strips. 3 times 7 is 21, and 2 times 10 is 20. Both match the question.
The key idea: the extra area is a strip. Divide it by its width and you get a side of the rectangle. Here that led us to 34.

board.text: 36 square tiles, all used, to make one rectangle.

spec.note: One way to use all 36 tiles: 4 by 9

beats.say: Rahul has 36 square tiles. He uses all of them to make one rectangle. How many different rectangles can he make?
Every rectangle uses all 36 tiles: rows times tiles in a row is 36. So we need pairs of numbers that multiply to 36.
Let's list them in order so we don't miss any. 1 by 36. 2 by 18. 3 by 12. 4 by 9.

choices: No, a square is not a rectangle
ask.ifNot: Read the question again. It says a square counts as a rectangle here. So 6 by 6 goes on our list.

beats.say: 5 doesn't go into 36. Next is 6: 6 times 6 is 36. Does a 6 by 6 square count?
After 6 by 6 the pairs just turn round. 9 by 4 is the same rectangle as 4 by 9, so we stop here.
Count the list: 5 rectangles.
Two traps here. Leaving out the 6 by 6 square gives 4. Counting turned-round pairs again gives too many.
So: list the pairs in order, starting from 1, and stop when they begin to repeat. Here that gives 5.

board.text: A big square: 3 rows of 3 small squares.
How many squares of all sizes?

beats.say: A big square is divided into 3 rows of 3 equal small squares, like a noughts and crosses board. How many squares of all sizes are there?
The quick answer is 9. But the question says all sizes! So we count size by size. Small squares first: 3 rows of 3 is 9.

ask.ifNot: Slide a 2 by 2 block around the board. It fits top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right.

beats.say: Next, squares made of 4 small ones: a block 2 wide and 2 tall. How many of those can you find?

spec.note: A 2 by 2 block: 2 places across and 2 places down

beats.say: The block can sit in 2 places across and 2 places down. 2 times 2 is 4 of them.
And one more: the whole board is a square too. That is 1.
Add them up. 9 plus 4 plus 1 is 14.
There are 14 squares of all sizes.
When a question says all sizes, count each size in turn: small, medium, big. Then add.

board.text: 5 small squares joined in one row.
How many rectangles that are NOT squares?

beats.say: Five equal small squares are joined in a row to make a strip. Look at every shape made of one square or several neighbours. How many are rectangles that are not squares?
A single small square is a square, so those 5 don't count. We need shapes that are longer than they are tall.
Take 2 squares side by side. That is a rectangle. It can start at square 1, 2, 3 or 4. So there are 4 of them.

ask.ifNot: A shape 3 squares long can start at square 1, square 2 or square 3. If it started any later it would poke out of the strip.

beats.say: Now 3 squares side by side. In how many places can that start?
3 long: 3 shapes. 4 long: 2 shapes. And the whole strip, 5 long: just 1.
See the pattern? 4, 3, 2, 1. Add them up and we get 10.
So 10 of the shapes are rectangles that are not squares.
The trap is counting only the shapes 2 long, or adding in the 5 single squares. Be orderly: one length at a time.

board.text: Which statement about quadrilaterals is true?

beats.say: Here are four statements about quadrilaterals, and only one is true. Let's test each one by hunting for a shape that breaks it.

ask.ifNot: A rectangle's sides are not all equal. The shape with four equal sides that leans over, like a diamond, is the rhombus.

beats.say: First: four equal sides is always a square. Can you think of a shape with four equal sides that is not a square?
A leaning rhombus breaks it. So the first statement is not true.
Second: four right angles always means four equal sides. Think of a long rectangle, like a door. Four right angles, but not four equal sides.
Third: two pairs of equal sides is always a parallelogram. This one sounds right! But think of a kite.
In a kite the equal sides sit next to each other, and no sides are parallel. So the third is not true either.

board.text: 4 equal sides → opposite sides parallel: TRUE

beats.say: Last: four equal sides always means opposite sides are parallel. Four equal sides make a rhombus, or a square. In both, opposite sides are parallel.
So the true statement is the last one: four equal sides always gives parallel opposite sides.
To test the word always, look for one shape that breaks the rule. If no shape can break it, the rule holds.

board.text: 4 angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°.
Which can a quadrilateral NOT have?

beats.say: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees. Which of these can a quadrilateral not have?
Let's test each choice with real numbers. Four right angles: a right angle is 90 degrees, and 4 times 90 is 360. That's a square. Possible.
Three obtuse angles: obtuse means more than 90. Try 100, 100 and 100. That makes 300, so the fourth angle is 60. Possible!
Two right angles and one acute angle: try 90, 90 and 80. The fourth would be 100. Possible.

ask.ifNot: 4 angles of exactly 90 make 360. If every one of them is smaller than 90, the total has to be smaller too.

beats.say: Now four acute angles. Acute means less than 90. If all four are less than 90, what can we say about their total?
Even 89, 89, 89 and 89 fall short of 360. But a quadrilateral needs exactly 360. So this can never happen.
A quadrilateral cannot have four acute angles.
The surprise is that three obtuse angles are fine. Don't trust a feeling: try real numbers and add them up.

board.text: Perimeter of each strip = 40 cm. Area of square = ?

spec.note: 4 equal strips. Each strip has a perimeter of 40 cm

beats.say: A square sheet is cut into 4 equal strips by cuts parallel to one side. Each strip has a perimeter of 40 centimetres. What is the area of the square?
Look at one strip. Its long side is the full side of the square. Its short side is a quarter of that. So the long side is 4 times the short side.
Half of the strip's perimeter is one long side plus one short side. Half of 40 is 20.

ask.ifNot: The long side counts as 4 short sides. Add the short side itself, and that is 4 and 1 more.

beats.say: Long plus short is 20, and the long side is 4 shorts. So how many short sides make 20?
4 shorts and 1 short make 5 shorts. 20 divided by 5 is 4. The short side is 4 centimetres.
The long side is 4 times 4, which is 16. And that is the side of the square.
Area of the square: 16 times 16. 16 times 10 is 160, and 16 times 6 is 96. Together, 256.
So the area of the square sheet is 256 square centimetres.
The trap is taking 20 as the side of the square. 20 is a long side and a short side together.
Check a strip: 16 plus 4 is 20, and double 20 is 40. It fits, so 256 is our area.

board.text: Which can be the area: 54, 36, 96 or 75 sq cm?

spec.note: The length is 3 times the breadth

beats.say: The length of a rectangle is 3 times its breadth, and both are whole numbers. Which of these can be its area: 54, 36, 96 or 75?
Picture it. The length is 3 breadths, so the rectangle is 3 squares in a row. Each square is one breadth by one breadth.
So if we divide the area by 3, we get the area of one of those squares. Let's divide each choice by 3.

ask.ifNot: Try a number times itself. 5 times 5 is 25. No whole number times itself makes 18, 12 or 32.

beats.say: 18, 12, 32 and 25. One square must be a whole number times itself. Which of these is?
25 is 5 times 5. So the breadth is 5 centimetres, and the length is 3 times 5, which is 15.
Check: 15 times 5 is 75.
So the area can be 75 square centimetres.
Watch out for 36. It is 6 times 6, but that is a square sheet, not a rectangle 3 times as long as it is wide.
So: divide the area by 3, and look for a number times itself. Only 75 passes the test.

board.text: A 4 cm square is cut from one corner. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: A 4 cm square is cut from one corner. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: A square card has sides of 10 centimetres. A small square of side 4 centimetres is cut away from one corner. What is the perimeter of the card that is left?
Let's walk round the card that is left and list its edges. Two edges weren't touched by the cut. They are still 10 centimetres each.
The other two edges each lost 4 centimetres at the cut corner. 10 minus 4 is 6. So they are 6 centimetres each.

choices: Yes, that is all of them
No, the notch has 2 new edges
ask.ifNot: Run your finger round the notch in the picture. The cut leaves two fresh edges on the inside, each 4 centimetres long.

beats.say: Is that all the edges? Look at the corner where the small square used to be.
The notch has two new edges, each 4 centimetres. So the card has six edges now: 10, 10, 6, 6, 4 and 4.
Add them up. 10 plus 10 plus 6 plus 6 plus 4 plus 4 makes 40.
The perimeter of the card that is left is 40 centimetres.
Surprise! The whole square was 4 times 10, which is 40 too. The two new edges exactly replace the two pieces we lost.
Cutting out a corner changes the area, but here not the perimeter. Always walk round and count every edge.

board.text: Rectangle: length 26 cm, breadth 20 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 26 centimetres long and 20 centimetres broad. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 20 rows of 26, so we multiply 26 by 20.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 20 rows, with 26 in every row. So the area is length times breadth.
20 is 2 tens. So first we find 26 times 2. That is 52.
26 times 20 is 10 times as big as that. So it is 520.
There it is: the area is 520 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 520 squares shared into 20 rows gives 26 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the breadth, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Rectangle: length 14 cm, breadth 7 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 14 centimetres long and 7 centimetres broad. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two breadths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a breadth, then another length and another breadth. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one breadth first. 14 plus 7 is 21.
Careful: 21 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two breadths, so we double it. 2 times 21 is 42.
There it is: the perimeter is 42 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 14, 7, 14, 7. Together they make 42.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the breadth, then double.

board.text: Rectangle: length 21 cm, breadth 20 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 21 centimetres long and 20 centimetres broad. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two breadths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a breadth, then another length and another breadth. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one breadth first. 21 plus 20 is 41.
Don't stop at 41. That is just one length and one breadth, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 41 is 82.
So the perimeter is 82 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 21, 20, 21, 20. Together they make 82.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the breadth, then double.

board.text: Rectangle: length 13 cm, breadth 6 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 13 centimetres long and 6 centimetres broad. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 6 rows of 13, so we multiply 13 by 6.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 6 rows, with 13 in every row. So the area is length times breadth.
13 times 6 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 13 into 10 and 3.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 10 times 6 is 60. And 3 times 6 is 18. Now we put the two parts together. What is 60 plus 18?
60 plus 18 makes 78.
There it is: the area is 78 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 78 squares shared into 6 rows gives 13 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by breadth. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.

board.text: Rectangle: length 7 cm, breadth 3 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 7 centimetres long and 3 centimetres broad. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two breadths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a breadth, then another length and another breadth. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one breadth first. 7 plus 3 is 10.
Careful: 10 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two breadths, so we double it. 2 times 10 is 20.
So the perimeter is 20 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 7, 3, 7, 3. Together they make 20.
Remember the plan. Length plus breadth takes you halfway round. Double it for the whole perimeter.

board.text: Rectangle: length 24 cm, breadth 12 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 24 centimetres long and 12 centimetres broad. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 12 rows of 24, so we multiply 24 by 12.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 12 rows, with 24 in every row. So the area is length times breadth.
24 times 12 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 12 into 10 and 2.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 24 times 10 is 240. And 24 times 2 is 48. Now we put the two parts together. What is 240 plus 48?
Add them up: 240 plus 48 is 288.
There it is: the area is 288 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 288 squares shared into 12 rows gives 24 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the breadth, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Rectangle 4 cm by 1 cm, cut into 4 equal squares.

spec.note: Cut into 4 equal squares

beats.say: A rectangle 4 centimetres long and 1 centimetre broad is cut into 4 equal squares. How much more is the total perimeter of the squares than the perimeter of the rectangle?
First the squares. The rectangle is 1 centimetre broad, so each square has a side of 1 centimetre. Its perimeter is 4 times 1, which is 4.
There are 4 squares. 4 times 4 is 16 centimetres in all.
Now the rectangle. Length plus breadth is 4 plus 1, which is 5. Double it: 10 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Each cut opens up two fresh edges, one on each side of the cut. Those edges were hidden inside the rectangle before.

beats.say: The squares have 16 and the rectangle has 10. The pieces are the same paper! So why do the squares have more?
Every cut makes new edges. So the squares have more perimeter. 16 minus 10 is 6.
The squares have 6 centimetres more.
Check with the cuts. 3 cuts, each making 2 new edges of 1 centimetre. 3 times 2 is 6. It matches!
Read the last words of the question carefully. It asks how much more, so we find both totals and subtract.

board.text: Square and equilateral triangle: equal perimeter.

beats.say: A square and an equilateral triangle have equal perimeters. Which shape has the longer side?
There are no numbers here, so let's choose our own. Say both perimeters are 12 centimetres. 12 is easy to share.
The square shares 12 among 4 equal sides. 12 divided by 4 is 3.

ask.ifNot: The triangle has 3 equal sides, so we share 12 into 3 parts, not 4.

beats.say: The triangle shares the same 12 among only 3 sides. What is each side of the triangle?
12 divided by 3 is 4. So the triangle's side is 4 centimetres.
3 is less than 4. The square's side is shorter than the triangle's side.
Why? It is like sharing a chocolate bar. Share the same bar among more friends, and each piece is smaller.

board.text: Side of square < side of triangle

beats.say: So the true statement is: side of square is less than side of triangle.
When a question has no numbers, try an easy number of your own. Then look for the reason behind what you see.

spec.note: The length is 2 breadths

beats.say: The length of a rectangle is twice its breadth, and both are natural numbers. Which of these can be its perimeter: 232, 138, 334 or 146?

ask.ifNot: Each length counts as 2 breadths. So we add 2 and 1 and 2 and 1.

beats.say: Let's count the perimeter in breadths. One length is 2 breadths. Walk round: 2, then 1, then 2, then 1. How many breadths is that?
2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6. So the perimeter is 6 breadths. It must be in the 6 times table!

board.text: 6 times table: even, and in the 3 times table

beats.say: A number in the 6 times table is even, and also in the 3 times table. All four choices are even, so we test for 3.
Here is a handy test for 3: add the digits. For 232, 2 plus 3 plus 2 is 7. 7 is not in the 3 times table, so 232 is out.
For 138, 1 plus 3 plus 8 is 12. 12 is in the 3 times table. So 138 works!
Check the other two. 3 plus 3 plus 4 is 10, and 1 plus 4 plus 6 is 11. Neither is in the 3 times table.
So the perimeter can be 138 centimetres.
Let's make sure. 138 divided by 6 is 23. So the breadth is 23 and the length is 46. Both natural numbers.
The big idea: turn the whole perimeter into breadths. Then you know which times table it must be in. Only 138 fits.

spec.note: Perimeter = 14 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a square is 14 centimetres. What could one side measure?
A square has 4 equal sides, so we share 14 among 4. Half of 14 is 7, and half of 7 is 3.5.
So the side is 3.5 centimetres. That is 3 whole centimetres and half a centimetre more.

ask.ifNot: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. Half a centimetre is half of 10.

beats.say: But 3.5 centimetres is not written like that in the choices. How many millimetres make half a centimetre?
Half of 10 is 5. So half a centimetre is 5 millimetres.
One side is 3 centimetres and 5 millimetres.
Careful with one choice: 3.5 millimetres. The number looks right, but the unit is far too small. Always read the unit.
Check: 4 sides of 3.5 make 14. It fits.

board.text: Rectangle 3 cm by 1 cm, cut into 3 squares.

spec.note: Cut into 3 square pieces

beats.say: A rectangle 3 centimetres long and 1 centimetre broad is cut into 3 square pieces. How much more is the total perimeter of the squares than the perimeter of the rectangle?
Each piece is a square of side 1 centimetre. One square has a perimeter of 4 times 1, which is 4.

ask.ifNot: One square has 4 centimetres. There are 3 squares, so we need 3 lots of 4.

beats.say: There are 3 squares. What is their total perimeter?
3 times 4 is 12 centimetres.
Now the rectangle. 3 plus 1 is 4, and double is 8 centimetres.
12 minus 8 is 4. The squares have 4 centimetres more.
Where did the extra come from? Each cut opens 2 new edges of 1 centimetre. 2 cuts, so 2 times 2 is 4. It matches.
Cutting never changes the area, but it always adds perimeter, because new edges appear.

board.text: Square: perimeter 36 cm. 3 squares joined in a row.

spec.note: Each square has a perimeter of 36 cm

beats.say: A square has a perimeter of 36 centimetres. Three such squares are joined in a straight row to make a rectangle. What is the rectangle's perimeter?
Tempting idea: 3 squares, so 3 times 36. Do you think that's right? Think about the edges where the squares join.
That's the trap! Where two squares join, those edges end up inside the rectangle. They are not on the boundary any more.
So let's find the real sides. One side of a square is 36 divided by 4, which is 9 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Three sides of 9 centimetres sit end to end along the length. So we need 3 lots of 9.

beats.say: Three squares side by side. How long is the rectangle?
3 times 9 is 27. The rectangle is 27 centimetres long and still 9 centimetres wide.
27 plus 9 is 36. That is halfway round. Double it: 72.
The perimeter of the rectangle is 72 centimetres.
So when shapes are joined, don't add their perimeters. Find the new sides, then go round the outside.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter = 42 cm, length = 13 cm. Breadth = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = 42 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a rectangle is 42 centimetres, and its length is 13 centimetres. What is the breadth?
The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths. So half of it is one length plus one breadth. Half of 42 is 21.

ask.ifNot: 42 is the whole way round. One length and one breadth make only 21. So we take 13 away from 21.

beats.say: Length plus breadth is 21, and the length is 13. How do we find the breadth?
21 minus 13 is 8.
The breadth is 8 centimetres.
The trap is taking 13 from 42 straight away. That removes one length, but another length and two breadths are still there.

So the length and breadth can be 10.5 metres and 5.5 metres.
Sides don't have to be whole numbers. Halve the perimeter, then look for the pair that adds up to it: 10.5 and 5.5.

board.text: Rectangle: length 19 cm, width 16 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 19 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 19 plus 16 is 35.
Don't stop at 35. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 35 is 70.
There it is: the perimeter is 70 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 19, 16, 19, 16. Together they make 70.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: This rectangle's sides are written with letters. The length is 2 m plus 5 n. The breadth is m minus 3 n. We want the perimeter.
Letters don't change the plan. Perimeter is still length plus breadth, then doubled.
First add the length and the breadth. Collect the m's together: 2 m and 1 more m make 3 m.

ask.ifNot: The breadth has minus 3 n, so we take 3 n away from the 5 n. 5 take away 3 is 2.

beats.say: Now the n's. We have 5 n, and then minus 3 n. What is left?
5 n take away 3 n leaves 2 n. So length plus breadth is 3 m plus 2 n. That is halfway round.
Now double everything. 2 times 3 m is 6 m. And 2 times 2 n is 4 n.
Careful: the 2 multiplies both parts, the 3 m and the 2 n. Doubling only one of them is the classic slip.
So the perimeter is 6 m plus 4 n.
With letters or with numbers, the plan is the same: add the two sides, then double.

spec.note: Perimeter = 40 cm

beats.say: This rectangle's sides use a letter, a. The length is 3 a minus 5 and the breadth is a plus 5. The perimeter is 40 centimetres. We must find a.
Start with what we know about perimeters. Length plus breadth is half of the perimeter. Half of 40 is 20.

ask.ifNot: Minus 5 means take 5 away. Plus 5 puts 5 back. So together they do nothing at all.

beats.say: Now add the length and the breadth. 3 a and 1 more a make 4 a. But what happens to the minus 5 and the plus 5?
Minus 5 and plus 5 cancel. So length plus breadth is just 4 a.
Here's the trap: 4 a is only halfway round. So 4 a equals 20, not 40.
4 times what makes 20? We divide 20 by 4.
20 divided by 4 is 5. So a is 5.
Check. The length is 3 times 5 minus 5, which is 10. The breadth is 5 plus 5, which is 10 too.
10 plus 10 is 20, and double 20 is 40. That is our perimeter, so a equals 5 works!

board.text: Field: 350 m long, 120 m wide. Sam runs 10 rounds.

spec.note: Ten rounds of the field = ?

beats.say: Sam ran ten rounds of a rectangular field, 350 metres long and 120 metres wide. What total distance did Sam run?
One round is the perimeter of the field. One length and one width: 350 plus 120 is 470.

choices: No, it is half a round
ask.ifNot: 350 plus 120 takes Sam along one long side and one short side. He is at the opposite corner, only halfway round.

beats.say: Is 470 metres one full round?
470 is only halfway. Double it for a full round: 2 times 470 is 940 metres.
Sam ran ten rounds. 10 times 940 is 9400 metres.
Now look at the choices. 9400 metres isn't there, but some are in kilometres. 1000 metres make 1 kilometre.
9400 divided by 1000 is 9.4. So Sam ran 9.4 kilometres.
Three things to watch here: double for the full round, times 10 for ten rounds, and change the unit at the end.

board.text: Length + breadth = 12 cm. Length − breadth = 2 cm.

spec.note: Length + breadth = 12 cm. They differ by 2 cm

beats.say: The length and breadth of a rectangle add up to 12 centimetres, and they differ by 2 centimetres. We want the area.
Careful: 12 and 2 are not the sides. They are the sum and the difference. First we must find the two sides.
The length is the breadth and 2 more. So take that extra 2 away from 12. What is left is two equal breadths.

ask.ifNot: 10 is two equal breadths together. Halve it to get one breadth.

beats.say: Two breadths make 10. So what is one breadth?
Half of 10 is 5. The breadth is 5 centimetres. The length is 2 more, which is 7.
Check the clues: 7 plus 5 is 12, and 7 minus 5 is 2. Both fit.
Now the area: 7 times 5 is 35.
The area is 35 square centimetres.
So with a sum and a difference: take the difference off, halve what is left, and you have the smaller side.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a square with sides of 9 centimetres. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Count the sides of the square in the picture. There are 4 of them, each 9 centimetres. So the walk is 4 lots of 9.

beats.say: A square has 4 sides, and they are all the same length. So which sum gives the whole walk?
4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times the side.
That is 4 lots of 9, and 4 times 9 is 36.
There it is: the perimeter is 36 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking the four sides one at a time. 9, 9, 9, 9. Together they make 36.
So, for the perimeter of any square: multiply the side by 4.
Four shapes: a square, an equilateral triangle, a rectangle and a rhombus. Which one has the least perimeter?
We can't tell by looking, so we work out all four. The square has 4 sides of 5.5 centimetres. 4 times 5.5 is 22.
The equilateral triangle has 3 sides of 6 centimetres. 3 times 6 is 18.
The rectangle is 5 centimetres by 3 centimetres. 5 plus 3 is 8, and double is 16.

ask.ifNot: A rhombus is like a square that has been pushed over. All 4 of its sides are equal.

beats.say: Last, the rhombus, with a side of 5 centimetres. How many equal sides does a rhombus have?
4 equal sides. 4 times 5 is 20.
Now compare: 22, 18, 16 and 20. The smallest is 16.

board.text: Least: the rectangle, 5 cm by 3 cm

beats.say: So the least perimeter belongs to the rectangle, 5 centimetres by 3 centimetres.
The triangle has the fewest sides, but that didn't make it the smallest. Work each one out before you compare.

board.text: Triangle's perimeter = perimeter of a square of side 6 cm

spec.note: An equilateral triangle has the same perimeter. Its side = ?

beats.say: An equilateral triangle has the same perimeter as a square of side 6 centimetres. What is the side of the triangle?
Start with the shape we know. The square has 4 sides of 6 centimetres. 4 times 6 is 24.

ask.ifNot: The triangle shares its 24 centimetres equally among 3 sides. So we divide 24 by 3.

beats.say: The triangle has the same perimeter, 24 centimetres. An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides. So how do we find one side?
24 divided by 3 is 8.
Each side of the triangle is 8 centimetres.
Notice that 8 is more than 6. The triangle has fewer sides to share the same perimeter, so each side is longer.
Check: 3 sides of 8 make 24, the same as the square.
Look at this square. Every side is 19 centimetres. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side goes round the edge. That is the perimeter. The little squares inside sit in 19 rows of 19, so we multiply 19 by 19.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the square filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
A square is as wide as it is long. So there are 19 rows, with 19 little squares in every row. The area is side times side.
19 times 19 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 19 as 10 and 9.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 19 times 10 is 190. And 19 times 9 is 171. Now we put the two parts together. What is 190 plus 171?
Add them up: 190 plus 171 is 361.
There it is: the area is 361 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 361 squares shared into 19 rows gives 19 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. Side times side is the area. 4 times the side is the perimeter. Don't mix them up!

board.text: Area of square = area of a rectangle 16 cm by 4 cm

spec.note: A square has the same area. Perimeter of the square = ?

beats.say: A square has the same area as a rectangle 16 centimetres long and 4 centimetres broad. We want the perimeter of the square.
Three steps here: the rectangle's area, then the square's side, then the square's perimeter. First, 16 times 4 is 64.

ask.ifNot: Try the times tables. 8 times 8 is 64. Halving 64 or dividing it by 4 does not give the side.

beats.say: The square's area is also 64. Area is side times side. Which number times itself makes 64?
8 times 8 is 64. So the side of the square is 8 centimetres.
Don't stop here! 8 is the side, but the question asks for the perimeter.
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 8 is 32.
The perimeter of the square is 32 centimetres.
Same area links the two shapes. From the area we find the side, and from the side we find the perimeter.

board.text: Perimeter of square = perimeter of a rectangle 16 cm by 4 cm

spec.note: A square has the same perimeter. Area of the square = ?

beats.say: A square has the same perimeter as a rectangle 16 centimetres long and 4 centimetres broad. We want the area of the square.
First the rectangle's perimeter. 16 plus 4 is 20. That is halfway round, so double it: 40.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides. Share the 40 centimetres among all 4 of them.

beats.say: The square's perimeter is also 40 centimetres. How long is each side of the square?
40 divided by 4 is 10. The side of the square is 10 centimetres.
Now the area: side times side. 10 times 10 is 100.
The area of the square is 100 square centimetres.
Here's something neat. The rectangle's area is 16 times 4, only 64. Same perimeter, but the square holds more.
Same perimeter links the two shapes. From the perimeter we find the side, then side times side gives 100.

board.text: Rectangle: length 12 cm, width 11 cm. Perimeter = ?

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, width 16 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 25 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 16 rows of 25, so we multiply 25 by 16.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 16 rows, with 25 in every row. So the area is length times width.

board.text: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are: ?

beats.say: In a parallelogram, what is true about the opposite sides?

ask.ifNot: Say it slowly: parallel, o, gram. The name begins with the word parallel.

beats.say: Listen to the name: parallelogram. Which word can you hear hiding inside it?
Parallel! Opposite sides run in the same direction, like railway tracks, and never meet.

spec.note: Each side is as long as the side facing it

beats.say: Now look at their lengths. In the picture, compare the top side with the bottom side, and the left side with the right side.
Each side is exactly as long as the side facing it. So opposite sides are equal as well.
So in a parallelogram, opposite sides are parallel and equal.
Two facts, and both are true. Don't settle for a choice that gets only one of them right.

board.text: In a rhombus, the axes of symmetry are: ?

spec.note: A rhombus

beats.say: A rhombus has axes of symmetry. Which lines are they?

board.text: Axis of symmetry = a fold line that matches

beats.say: An axis of symmetry is a fold line. Fold along it, and one half lands exactly on the other.

choices: No, an angle is not a line
ask.ifNot: An angle is a corner, the turn between two sides. We can only fold along a line.

beats.say: So an axis has to be a line we can fold along. Could an angle be an axis of symmetry?
Right, angles are out. Now try folding along a side. Nothing lands on anything, so the sides are out too.

spec.note: A rhombus folds onto itself in 2 ways

beats.say: Now fold the rhombus corner to corner, along a diagonal. All four sides are equal, so the two halves match exactly.

spec.note: The fold lines are its two diagonals

beats.say: The other diagonal works in the same way. So a rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry, and they are its diagonals.
Remember the paper test: if you can fold along the line and the halves match, it is an axis of symmetry.
Four statements about shapes. Only one is true. Let's test each one.
Every rhombus is a square? A rhombus has four equal sides, but it can lean over like a diamond. Then it has no right angles. Not true.
Every parallelogram is a rectangle? A parallelogram can lean over too. A rectangle needs four right angles. Not true.

choices: No, it is longer than it is wide
ask.ifNot: A door is much taller than it is wide. A square needs all four sides to be the same length.

beats.say: Every rectangle is a square? Think of a door. It is a rectangle, but are its four sides equal?
A long rectangle is not a square. So that one is not true either.
Every square is a rectangle? A rectangle only needs four right angles. Does every square have four right angles? Yes, always!

board.text: Every square is a rectangle: TRUE

beats.say: So the true statement is: every square is a rectangle. A square is a special rectangle, one with equal sides.
The trick with the word every: hunt for one shape that breaks the rule. If you find one, the statement is not true.

board.text: Rectangle: length 26 cm, width 24 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 26 centimetres long and 24 centimetres wide, and we want its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 24 rows of 26, so we multiply 26 by 24.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 24 rows of squares, and 26 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
26 times 24 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 24 as 20 and 4.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 26 times 20 is 520. And 26 times 4 is 104. Now we put the two parts together. What is 520 plus 104?
520 plus 104 makes 624.
There it is: the area is 624 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 624 squares shared into 24 rows gives 26 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Exactly one pair of parallel sides. It is called a: ?

spec.note: Exactly one pair of parallel sides

beats.say: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it called?
Parallel sides run in the same direction and never meet, like railway tracks. Let's count the parallel pairs in each shape.
A parallelogram has two pairs: top with bottom, and left with right. A rhombus has two pairs as well.

ask.ifNot: Picture a kite in the sky. Its sides all slant in different directions, so none of them are parallel.

beats.say: What about a kite? Its equal sides sit next to each other. Does a kite usually have any parallel sides?
A kite usually has no parallel sides at all.
That leaves the trapezium. Its top and bottom are parallel, but its other two sides are not. Exactly one pair!
So the shape is a trapezium.
The word exactly matters. Two pairs is too many. We want one pair and no more.

board.text: A kite has how many axes of symmetry?

spec.note: A kite

beats.say: Here is a kite. How many axes of symmetry does it have?

spec.note: Two short sides together, two long sides together

beats.say: A kite has two short sides that meet at one end, and two long sides that meet at the other end.

spec.note: Fold along this line: one half lands on the other

beats.say: An axis of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves match. Fold the kite along its length, from one end corner to the other.
One half lands exactly on the other. Short side on short side, long side on long side. That is 1 axis.

ask.ifNot: One part has the two short sides and the other part has the two long sides. When you fold, a short side lands on a long side.

beats.say: Now fold it the other way, across the middle, joining the two side corners. Do the halves match?

spec.note: This fold puts a short side on a long side

beats.say: A short side would land on a long side. So that fold does not match.

spec.note: 1 axis of symmetry

beats.say: A kite has just 1 axis of symmetry.
A rhombus has 2 and a square has 4. The kite, with its two different pairs of sides, has only the one.
Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90 degrees, 85 degrees and 110 degrees. What is the fourth angle?
The key fact: the four angles of a quadrilateral always add up to 360 degrees.
Add the three we know. 90 plus 85 is 175. Then 175 plus 110 is 285.

ask.ifNot: The fourth angle is whatever is left of the 360 after the other three. To find what is left, we subtract.

beats.say: Three angles use up 285 of the 360 degrees. What do we do to find the fourth?
360 minus 285. From 285 up to 300 is 15, and from 300 up to 360 is 60. 15 and 60 make 75.
The fourth angle is 75 degrees.
Check: 90, 85, 110 and 75 add up to 360.
Add the three you know, then take the total from 360. And add carefully: most slips happen in the adding.
The area of a square is 144 square centimetres. What is its side?
Area of a square is side times side. So we need a number that, multiplied by itself, gives 144.
Careful: this is not 144 divided by 4. Dividing by 4 is for a perimeter. Here we hunt for a number times itself.

ask.ifNot: 100 is less than 144. We need more area, so we need a longer side.

beats.say: Start with an easy one. 10 times 10 is 100. Is the side bigger or smaller than 10?
Bigger. Try 11: 11 times 11 is 121. Still too small.
Try 12: 12 times 12 is 144. That's it!
The side of the square is 12 centimetres.
To go from area back to the side, ask: which number times itself gives the area? Try, check, and adjust.

board.text: Rectangle: length 23 cm, width 7 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 23 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 7 rows of 23, so we multiply 23 by 7.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?

23 times 7 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 23 into 20 and 3.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 20 times 7 is 140. And 3 times 7 is 21. Now we put the two parts together. What is 140 plus 21?
140 plus 21 makes 161.
So the area is 161 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 161 squares shared into 7 rows gives 23 in each row. It fits!

board.text: Rectangle: area = 96 cm², length = 12 cm. Breadth = ?

beats.say: A rectangle has an area of 96 square centimetres and a length of 12 centimetres. What is its breadth?
Length times breadth gives the area. So 12 times the breadth is 96.

ask.ifNot: Multiplying made the 96. To go backwards from a multiplication, we divide.

beats.say: We know the answer to a multiplication and one of its numbers. How do we find the missing number?
Divide the area by the length: 96 divided by 12. Think: 12 times 8 is 96.
The breadth is 8 centimetres.
Check: 12 times 8 is 96. That is the area we were given.
A breadth of 8 makes sense: it must be a small number, because 12 lots of it make only 96.

spec.note: The diagonals AC and BD

beats.say: What is true about the two diagonals of a square?

board.text: Equal?  Cut in half?  Right angles?

beats.say: A diagonal joins opposite corners. A square has two of them, and they cross in the middle. We'll check three things.

spec.note: Like a rectangle: AC and BD are equal

beats.say: First: are they the same length? A square looks the same when you turn it. So one diagonal can't be longer than the other.

ask.ifNot: The crossing point is the very middle of the square. So it is the middle of each diagonal too.

beats.say: Second: bisect means cut exactly in half. The diagonals cross at the centre of the square. Does each one cut the other in half?
Yes. Each diagonal cuts the other exactly in half. They bisect each other.

spec.note: Like a rhombus: they cut each other in half at 90°

beats.say: Third: look at the corner where they cross. It is a square corner, a right angle.

board.text: Equal, and bisect at right angles

beats.say: So the diagonals of a square are equal, and they bisect each other at right angles.
A square gets the best of both: equal diagonals like a rectangle, and a right angle crossing like a rhombus.

board.text: Rectangle: length 9 cm, width 5 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 9 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 5 rows of 9, so we multiply 9 by 5.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 5 rows of squares, and 9 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
From the times tables, 9 times 5 is 45.
So the area is 45 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 45 squares shared into 5 rows gives 9 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, width 5 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 25 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 25 plus 5 is 30.
Careful: 30 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two widths, so we double it. 2 times 30 is 60.
So the perimeter is 60 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 25, 5, 25, 5. Together they make 60.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.
